title: How Groundhog Day Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the origins of Groundhog Day, a holiday blending ancient Celtic cross-quarter day traditions (Imbolc/Candlemas, February 2) with German and Pennsylvania groundhog and badger weather lore. They cover groundhog biology and hibernation, the Celtic cross-quarter days, Candlemas and its Christian conversion, the 1887 founding of the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club by newspaper editor Clymer Freas, Gobbler's Knob, the groundhog Phil and his handlers, the dawn ceremony and groundhog-speak, Phil's poor forecasting record, the film Groundhog Day and its filming in Woodstock, Illinois. The episode closes with a listener email about racism experienced by a Black listener and a jazz episode suggestion.

segments.title: Opening banter and groundhog facts
segments.summary: The hosts open the holiday special by joking about whether Groundhog Day is a holiday, then describe groundhogs: their size, lifespan, diet, whistling, climbing and swimming, and their hibernation and February mating behavior.

segments.title: Cross-quarter days and Celtic origins
segments.summary: The hosts explain the solstice and equinox calendar and the cross-quarter days in between. February 2 was the Celtic beginning of spring, called Imbolc, linked to Brigid, and was later Christianized as Candlemas, with candles blessed for the winter.

segments.title: Weather lore and farmers' predictions
segments.summary: Farmers used February 2 weather to predict late frosts. Sunshine on Candlemas meant more winter was coming, while overcast or gross weather meant spring was near. The hosts compare this to other folk weather signs such as woolly caterpillars and spider webs.

segments.title: Ancient Celts and the Indo-European migration
segments.summary: A digression on a New Yorker article about skeletons in a Himalayan lake, which discusses the spread of Indo-European steppe peoples and the more egalitarian Celts of Western Europe. The hosts also mention the film Midsummer.

segments.title: German badger tradition and Pennsylvania origins
segments.summary: Germans had a tradition of waking a badger to see if it would return to its burrow as a sign of weather. Settlers in Pennsylvania adapted it to groundhogs, since there were no badgers in America.

segments.title: Clymer Freas and the first Groundhog Day in 1887
segments.summary: Clymer Freas, editor of the Punxsutawney Spirit, published a line in 1886 about groundhog day and the first celebration was held in 1887. Freas helped form the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club in 1899, made of groundhog hunters who ate groundhogs. The first event was at Gobbler's Knob. An earlier diary mention by James Morris is also noted.

segments.title: Punxsutawney Phil and the groundhog club
segments.summary: Phil is the groundhog of record, said to be the same groundhog since 1887 because he drinks a dandelion punch each summer. The hosts discuss the name, the top hats, the inner circle of volunteers and handlers, and the Ugga-style succession of groundhogs.

segments.title: The Gobbler's Knob ceremony and groundhog-speak
segments.summary: Phil is taken from his burrow at night to a stump stage at Gobbler's Knob, where thousands gather overnight. The club's president translates Phil's rhyming pronouncement at dawn. Phil's forecasting record is described as roughly 30 to 40 percent accurate, and the handlers, not Phil, make the predictions.

segments.title: Groundhog Day the movie and Woodstock filming
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1993 film Groundhog Day, its time-loop premise, its impact on culture and deja vu, the screenwriter's ten-thousand-year original idea, and that it was filmed in Woodstock, Illinois rather than Punxsutawney.
